argument_summary: The admissible record supports a narrower certification case than a clean no-limitations claim. Aggregate launch-readiness evidence is real: the release clears readiness by 2.2 points, has no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and passes general support, latency, and rollback checks. The same record also establishes that refund-policy summarization is a named deployment context whose evals are not in the packet, so that area must be treated as an unknown coverage gap rather than as passed. The supportable position is therefore certification for overall launch readiness only if the packet and model-card treatment are framed to disclose that named gap instead of implying full coverage.
claims_about_business_cost: The governance issue here is overstatement in the certification narrative, not absence of launch-readiness evidence. Treating this as a disclosure-and-wording correction rather than an escalation case preserves launch velocity without changing the substantive risk picture established by the packet.
claims_about_policy: The policy does not require every named context to be proven passed by the existing aggregate and operational checks; it does require that material limitations and evaluation gaps for named deployment contexts be disclosed unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance. On the admissible evidence, a clean certification statement is not supportable, but a narrower certification rationale aligned to explicit disclosure of the refund-policy summarization gap is consistent with the policy text and with the cited model-card and risk-measurement guidance.
concessions: The draft model-card statement that there are no known enterprise refund workflow limitations is not supported by the admissible evidence.
The missing refund-policy summarization evals cannot be treated as passed merely because no completed test failed.
The current record does not prove that final disclosure or approved risk acceptance was completed before certification.
